title: AI Systems
summary: A repository-backed orchestration system that separates persona roles, shared context, durable work state, and live tool state so complex AI-assisted work can be routed and resumed without turning one orchestrator into every specialist.

sources.label: Persona-Library repository operating contract
Persona-Library Work Order contract
Shared problem-context contract
Riley universal Current Work orchestration Work Order

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: The system coordinates reusable Personas, Skills, Playbooks, Tools, project-scoped Work Orders, and a concise Current Work index while preserving separate ownership boundaries. The orchestration layer is designed to keep complex work resumable without becoming the execution path for every specialist task.

evidence.note: Repository contract defines Riley as the default durable orchestration owner while selected Personas, Skills, Playbooks, Tool paths, or runtimes may execute directly.
Work Order guidance defines the durable coordination hierarchy and resume order.

sections.title: Context
sections.body: Non-trivial AI-assisted work can cross agents, repositories, tools, approvals, and interruptions. Durable records need enough context to resume, while freshness-sensitive systems such as GitHub checks, permissions, and deployments must remain authoritative in their own systems rather than being copied into a tracker that can go stale.

evidence.note: Defines Current Work, Work Orders, and live systems as separate layers with different freshness responsibilities.

items.title: Riley Morgan — orchestration
items.summary: Owns durable routing and continuity for substantial workstreams, reconciling state at creation, material rerouting, handoff, major blockers, and completion.

items.title: Domain specialists — execution
items.summary: Selected Personas, Skills, Playbooks, Tool paths, and runtimes execute the work directly when they own the relevant capability; Riley does not become a mandatory execution hop.

items.title: Coordinator — shared context
items.summary: For multi-Persona work, one coordinator records attributable contributions, evidence status, decisions, dispositions, gates, and handoffs in the shared problem context.

evidence.note: Records the durable-orchestration invariant and direct-execution boundary.
Defines coordinator/single-writer behavior and attributable participant contributions.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: Two failure modes shaped the architecture: making the orchestrator perform every execution step adds redundant coordination and blurs domain ownership, while mirroring volatile operational state into durable trackers makes those trackers look complete but quickly stale.

evidence.note: Explicitly rejects a mandatory Riley execution hop and a second orchestration database.
Explicitly says not to mirror volatile live state into Current Work.

sections.title: Exploration
sections.body: The working model separated three kinds of state: a concise cross-agent index, a detailed project recovery packet, and the live systems that own current operational truth. Multi-Persona collaboration was treated as a separate shared-context problem with a single writer, attributable contributions, and a quality gate instead of an informal panel transcript.

evidence.note: Documents the Current Work → Work Order → live systems hierarchy.
Documents the shared-context lifecycle, evidence ledger, dispositions, and quality gate.

items.title: Current Work
items.summary: A concise cross-thread index containing objective, owner, route, next action, blocker, checkpoint, and authoritative links.

items.title: Work Orders
items.summary: Project-scoped execution and recovery packets that preserve scope, constraints, decisions, phase state, evidence, handoffs, validation, and the next safe action.

items.title: Problem context
items.summary: A bounded shared source of truth for multi-Persona contributions, evidence status, decisions, artifacts, quality gates, and handoffs.

items.title: Live systems
items.summary: GitHub, deployments, permissions, and other freshness-sensitive systems remain the authority for state that can change independently of a checkpoint.

items.title: Reconciliation points
items.summary: Durable orchestration state is updated at material lifecycle boundaries rather than after every remote operation.

evidence.note: Defines the responsibilities and lifecycle of Current Work, Work Orders, and live-system refresh.
Defines the multi-Persona context and completion gate.

items.title: Keep orchestration separate from execution
items.summary: Riley remains the continuity and routing layer; the smallest relevant specialist path performs the actual work.

items.title: Do not create a second orchestration database
items.summary: The existing Current Work tracker remains the cross-agent index and Work Orders remain the detailed recovery packet.

items.title: Keep volatile authority live
items.summary: Fresh GitHub, CI, deployment, permission, and similar state is selectively refreshed instead of copied into durable notes.

items.title: Require attributable collaboration
items.summary: Multi-Persona work uses a single-writer context, explicit evidence status, contribution dispositions, and a concrete solution-quality gate.

evidence.note: Captures the placement decision and six orchestration invariants.
Captures attribution, disposition, handoff, and quality-gate decisions.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.body: The documented operating model now provides an explicit resume order, clear orchestration versus execution boundaries, a reusable handoff packet, evidence-status rules, contribution dispositions, and completion gates. Repository validation for the Riley continuity change passed at the recorded implementation checkpoint. This case study does not claim measured productivity, quality, or cost improvements.

evidence.note: Completion evidence records the implemented continuity contract and passing repository validation run.
Provides the reusable handoff and solution-quality gate contracts.

sections.title: Reflection
sections.body: The durable design move was separating control-plane continuity from specialist execution, and stable recovery state from freshness-sensitive operational truth. That makes the system easier to resume and inspect without pretending a tracker is the live system. This reflection is limited to the documented operating model and recorded implementation evidence; no efficiency metric is asserted here.

evidence.note: The state hierarchy and resume order support this architectural reflection.
The recorded placement review explicitly avoids duplicate orchestration infrastructure and redundant execution hops.

curationNotes: Synthesized from current Persona-Library contracts and completed orchestration work; it is not user research.
No productivity, cost, quality, or adoption metric is claimed because no attributable measurement was found in the source set.
Published without screenshots; add only source-approved visuals in a later media review.

title: UI Design Practices
summary: A staged design-to-implementation practice for turning an ambiguous portfolio redesign into information architecture, visual tokens, interaction contracts, reusable components, and browser-verifiable behavior.

sources.label: Portfolio redesign implementation plan
Portfolio interaction-spec and component-builder work
Portfolio DESIGN.md contract
Persona-Library Expert UX Design Practice
Persona-Library Project Context and Reference Routing

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: The portfolio redesign was organized as a sequence of inspectable design and engineering contracts: information architecture first, then visual system and navigation, then motion, then a shared case-study slice. Each phase had a concrete artifact and verification boundary before the next dependent layer was added.

evidence.note: Defines the phased redesign plan and handoff model.

sections.title: Context
sections.body: The starting portfolio already had routes, fixtures, a local harness, content imports, and a design contract. The redesign needed to change hierarchy and presentation without publishing draft case-study claims, duplicating navigation components, adding unnecessary dependencies, or breaking the existing admin/content boundaries.

evidence.note: Defines redesign boundaries, anti-goals, and publication constraints.
Documents the implemented shell, motion, component, accessibility, and verification contracts.

items.title: Hiring managers and design leadership
items.summary: Primary evaluation audience for fast understanding of positioning, representative work, design decisions, system thinking, and outcomes.

items.title: Potential consulting clients
items.summary: Secondary audience evaluating fit, problem-structuring ability, relevant examples, and a direct contact path.

items.title: UX and UI design roles
items.summary: Structure/content questions are separated from visual hierarchy, interaction states, responsive behavior, accessibility, and built-versus-designed QA.

evidence.note: Confirms primary and secondary portfolio audiences.
Defines conditional routing between UX structure work and UI hierarchy/interaction work.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: A portfolio redesign can become a styling exercise before the content model, route hierarchy, interaction states, and publication rules are clear. That makes visual polish difficult to evaluate and increases the chance of route-specific markup, hidden states, or unreviewed content appearing authoritative.

evidence.note: The UX practice requires reasoning, evidence, state coverage, traceability, and implementation QA rather than polished screens alone.
Phase order deliberately locks IA/content contracts before visual and motion implementation.

sections.title: Exploration
sections.body: The redesign explored a persistent left rail, a mobile drawer, recovery of the original orange accent, chapter-style route continuity, and a shared case-study model. The implementation favored native links, CSS variables, route groups, and CSS-first motion because those primitives covered the required behavior without a component or animation dependency.

evidence.note: Confirms the rail, drawer, cinematic direction, orange recovery, and shared case-study structure.
Documents the implemented shell and CSS-first motion contract.

items.title: Define structure before polish
items.summary: Visitor jobs, page modes, route contracts, section sequence, and publication boundaries are made explicit before visual implementation.

items.title: Turn visual direction into tokens
items.summary: Color, spacing, layout, and motion values live in semantic CSS variables and documented contracts instead of route-specific values.

items.title: Specify interaction behavior
items.summary: Important components document states, triggers, focus behavior, cancellation, responsive rules, accessibility, selectors, and verification.

items.title: Build shared components
items.summary: Public navigation and case-study rendering are reusable boundaries rather than repeated route markup.

items.title: Keep a deterministic harness
items.summary: Loading, empty, error, disabled, long-content, responsive, and reduced-motion behavior can be exercised without external services.

items.title: Validate the built experience
items.summary: Lint, typecheck, unit, browser, build, and local schema checks act as implementation gates rather than post-hoc cleanup.

evidence.note: Defines the interaction-spec and component-builder workflow.
Documents tokens, components, states, motion, responsive behavior, and verification.
Defines design practice from structure through implementation handoff and built QA.

items.title: Use a public route-group shell
items.summary: Public routes share persistent navigation while admin, API, and local harness surfaces remain outside the portfolio frame.

items.title: Recover the orange precisely
items.summary: The rendered original site was inspected and the accent was formalized as #F24C27, with a darker semantic ink token for small text contrast.

items.title: Keep motion CSS-first
items.summary: Short, interruptible CSS motion covers route entry, active state, drawer entry, and feedback without adding an animation dependency.

items.title: Make approval a route boundary
items.summary: Draft case studies can use the shared template locally, but public indexes and detail routes consume approval-filtered records only.

evidence.note: Documents shell ownership, accent provenance, motion decisions, and the shared case-study publication contract.
Establishes the staged implementation and draft-first constraints.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.body: The work produced documented route/content contracts, a persistent responsive navigation shell, semantic visual and motion tokens, reusable case-study components, and automated coverage for keyboard, mobile/tablet, reduced-motion, and publication-gate behavior. This case study describes implementation artifacts and checks; it does not claim hiring, conversion, or user-research outcomes.

evidence.note: Documents the implemented component and verification surface.
Records completed interaction-spec/component-builder verification on the portfolio foundation.
Defines the redesign acceptance criteria these implementation artifacts address.

sections.title: Reflection
sections.body: Separating structure, visual system, motion, content rendering, and verification into reviewable layers made each decision easier to trace to a user or system need. The remaining evidence gap is outcome validation: content approval, visual snapshots, release hardening, and real portfolio performance still need to be evaluated before this becomes a finished redesign story.

evidence.note: Requires traceable design reasoning, explicit unknowns, evaluation, and built QA.
Later phases explicitly cover editorial review, visual snapshots, and release hardening.

curationNotes: This is an implementation-practice case study, not a claim of user-research validation.
Outcome language is limited to inspectable artifacts and checks; hiring, conversion, usability, and business impact remain unmeasured.
Published without screenshots; add only source-approved visuals in a later media review.

title: Multi Product Integrations
summary: Designers were repeating similar workflow decisions across separate apps. I helped define shared patterns, Figma libraries and a layout starter that teams could reuse.
role: Primary contributor to workflow patterns, Figma libraries, and guidelines
scope: Work across engagements, including a real-estate example

sections.title: Why we needed common patterns
sections.body: Across different places I've worked, I've seen designers solve similar problems in separate apps. Teams were defining their own workflows even where the interactions overlapped, and a lot of that work was duplicated. We wanted to define common patterns that teams could reuse. This story brings together that work, with a real-estate engagement as one example.

evidence.note: Owner described duplicated design effort and workflows across apps, and clarified that this is a compilation of work across engagements.

sections.title: What I worked on
sections.body: I was a primary contributor to defining the workflow patterns and representing them in the system. In the real-estate engagement, I worked with three teammates. We each took on different parts of the patterns and iterated together. The definitions and libraries came out of our combined work, with my contribution focused on the workflow patterns and a layout starter for different problem spaces.

evidence.note: Owner confirmed his primary contribution, three teammates within the real-estate example, joint iteration, and creation of the layout starter.

sections.title: The decisions we kept repeating
sections.body: The work covered decisions designers make throughout an application: where close buttons belong, when to use a modal or drawer, and how to lay out information. We defined patterns for reading order, such as top to bottom and left to right, and for presenting labels and values horizontally or vertically.

We collaborated to identify scenarios where another team's process fit better than ours and brought those approaches into our system.

title: AI council for product decisions
summary: I built an AI council to examine product ideas through executive, manager and worker perspectives. Each persona assessed the same question against its own work and pain points.
role: Created the persona framework and AI council; compared perspectives and developed a use-case scenario
scope: Product ideas, data perspectives, and use-case development

sections.title: Questioning a product idea
sections.body: I wanted to explore whether a product idea would help an executive, a manager or a worker on the ground. Each would encounter the same idea from a different position, with different responsibilities and pain points. I created the council to bring those perspectives into product discovery.

evidence.note: Rick described creating an AI council to improve product decisions where previously the team could only assume. His example questions concerned usefulness in work, executive impact, and possible lack of usefulness.

sections.body: I built role profiles from industry practices and whitepapers. They connected the work people do, the decisions they own and what would make a tool useful or hard to trust. A separate Minnesota contractor profile generated with the same instructions shows what that looked like.

sections.title: What changed for product and UX
sections.body: The council helped me look past a general ‘this could be useful’ answer. I could ask whose work the idea actually served, where it might add friction and what each role needed from the data. I brought those perspectives together in a use-case scenario.

items.title: UX direction

title: Design Systems
summary: Teams redesigning legacy capabilities needed a more consistent starting point. I designed the platform framework as part of a shared library effort.
role: Platform framework design with cross-team collaboration

sections.title: A common starting point
sections.body: An established company was redesigning legacy capabilities and needed more consistent design across the work. Existing patterns included redundant approaches, so part of the job was deciding what teams could reuse. I designed the platform framework as part of a collaborative effort to establish a core library and lightweight governance. The library brought reusable design decisions into a common starting point for the teams involved.

evidence.note: Imported summary establishes consistency and legacy-capability goals; discovery establishes redundant patterns. The source supports a shared team effort, not sole authorship of the whole library.

Scope identifies an established company reimagining legacy capabilities. Outcomes explicitly attributes platform framework design to Rick and names collaborators, a core library and lightweight governance.

sections.title: Choosing what to reuse
sections.body: We audited existing design patterns alongside user scenarios, then prioritized where to remove duplication and improve consistency. Stakeholder workshops helped us align the goals, while feedback from developers helped us understand what was feasible. Reviewing the patterns together gave us existing work to organize and refine into the library.

sections.body: The core library held reusable styles and tokens. Density needed guidance suited to the surface being designed, so we maintained a display marketing style guide alongside enterprise interface guidance. Those surfaces had different needs, even within the same system. Designers could start with shared foundations and use the density guidance that matched their surface. Keeping both sets of guidance in the system allowed reuse to accommodate those differences.

sections.body: We created a library of reusable screens that designers could duplicate and modify for a specific use case. A template carried an existing design into the new task, giving the designer a starting point they could adapt. We also defined patterns for onboarding, work creation and progression, asset and inventory management, and account configuration and settings. The templates provided screens to work from, while the patterns guided how users moved through recurring workflows. This gave designers reusable material at the level of a screen and the task it supported.

sections.body: The first redesign used a dark left rail. A later pilot replaced it with a horizontal header and serif headings, but I preferred the persistent rail and rejected the serif voice. I asked for the rail to return with a lighter treatment, keeping Work, Notes, About and Contact beside the reading column. The revision used warm, light surfaces and Inter throughout, with scale, weight and spacing handling the hierarchy. A permanent column would take too much of the reading width on a phone, so the built interface changed to a compact top bar and menu drawer. The destinations stayed the same. Opening the drawer moved keyboard focus into it, and Escape closed it and returned focus to the menu.

evidence.note: Accepted owner feedback and material decisions: persistent light/warm rail, sans typography, simplified Home. Does not establish Rick personally building rail code or choosing each implementation value.
Explains persistent orientation compared with the horizontal-header pilot and the content-primary lighter treatment.

Current PersonalPracticeShell confirms the shared destinations, menu drawer, focus entry/trap and Escape focus return. Responsive CSS replaces the fixed rail with a compact bar below 900px. These are agent-built behaviors.

sections.body: The agents rendered three palettes against the same portfolio pages: the existing warm colors, a less saturated warm option and a near-neutral option. Content, typography, layout and the original orange accent stayed fixed, so the comparison showed the background alongside the work it would surround. I chose the less saturated warm option. The original orange remained for active navigation and selected emphasis, with a darker orange for small text on light surfaces.

evidence.note: Defines three controlled palette candidates on actual content, with non-palette variables held steady. Mood/reading benefits remain hypotheses.
Records Rick choosing reduced-warm-chroma candidate B and the final static palette values.
